extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and definitions for detecting and using compactness in topology/metric spaces (open-cover, sequential, Heine–Borel, Lebesgue number, consequences), together with basic algebraic definitions for modules/vector spaces, bases, linear maps, and matrix representation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Closed subsets of sequentially compact sets are compact
rubrics_metrics.description: Closed subsets of sequentially compact sets are compact.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proposition 8.1.6 — Students are asked to prove this; it should follow easily from definitions (closedness preserves limits of convergent subsequences).

rubrics_metrics.name: Tychonoff’s theorem (product of compacts is compact)
rubrics_metrics.description: If X and Y are compact spaces, then so is X × Y.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Theorem 8.2.1 — stated here in the metric/elementary-product context; proof deferred to Problem 8E (elementary metric proof). Useful as a criterion to deduce compactness of boxes/finite products.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compactness of [0,1]
rubrics_metrics.description: [0,1] is compact.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Theorem 8.2.2 — sketched direct proof via nested interval / pigeonhole construction producing a Cauchy subsequence; students can use completeness to deduce convergence. See Problem 8F for Bolzano-Weierstrass approach.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bolzano–Weierstraß in R^n: closed and bounded criterion
rubrics_metrics.description: A subset of R^n is compact if and only if it is closed and bounded.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Theorem 8.2.3 — proof reduces to containing the set in a compact box (product of compact intervals) and then using that closed subsets of compact sets are compact. Warning/example: closed + bounded need not imply compact in arbitrary metric spaces (see discrete metric counterexample).

rubrics_metrics.name: Open cover / subcover definition
rubrics_metrics.description: An open cover of a topological space X is a (possibly infinite) collection of open sets {U_α} with X = ⋃ U_α. A subcover is a subcollection that still covers X.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Definition 8.3.1 — basis for the open-cover notion of compactness and for constructing finite subcovers in examples; motivates many proofs and counterexamples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quasicompact vs compact (Hausdorff requirement)
rubrics_metrics.description: A space X is quasicompact if every open cover has a finite subcover. It is compact if it is quasicompact and Hausdorff.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Definition 8.3.2 and Remark 8.3.3 — many authors omit the Hausdorff requirement; in metric-space contexts the Hausdorff condition is automatic. The distinction matters in general topology (e.g., cofinite topology examples).

rubrics_metrics.name: Sequential compactness ⇔ compactness in metric spaces
rubrics_metrics.description: For a metric space M, sequential compactness is equivalent to compactness (open-cover definition).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Theorem 8.3.5 — usefulness: sequential-argument proofs (subsequence extraction) and open-cover proofs are interchangeable in metric settings; proofs deferred to later sections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compact ⇒ totally bounded
rubrics_metrics.description: If M is compact then M is totally bounded.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proposition 8.4.1 — proof uses the open-cover approach: ε-neighborhoods around every point form a cover, so compactness gives a finite subcover, yielding finite ε-net. Typical usage: deducing precompactness properties from compactness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Images of compact sets under continuous maps are compact
rubrics_metrics.description: Let f : X → Y be continuous and X compact. Then f(img(X)) ⊆ Y is compact.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Theorem 8.4.2 — proof via pulling back an open cover of the image to an open cover of X and using finite subcover; also can be proven by sequential definitions. Key corollaries: extreme value theorem, intermediate value theorem.

rubrics_metrics.name: Extreme value theorem (continuous functions on compact attain maxima)
rubrics_metrics.description: If X is compact and f : X → R is continuous, then f achieves a maximum (and minimum) value on X.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Corollary 8.4.4 — follows from compactness of image of f and closed/boundedness in R. Typical exam/homework result demonstrating usefulness of compactness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intermediate value theorem for continuous maps from [0,1]
rubrics_metrics.description: For continuous f : [0, 1] → R, the image of f is an interval [a,b] for some a ≤ b.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Corollary 8.4.5 — argument: image is compact (closed and bounded) and connected when domain is [0,1], hence a single closed interval; full proof uses least upper bound property as needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Continuous on compact ⇒ uniformly continuous
rubrics_metrics.description: If M is compact and f : M → N is continuous (between metric spaces), then f is uniformly continuous.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proposition 8.4.9 — proof by contradiction using sequences and compactness (extract convergent subsequences, derive contradiction with images staying ε apart). Shows that in compact domains, δ can be chosen independent of base point.

rubrics_metrics.name: Uniform continuity definition
rubrics_metrics.description: f : M → N is uniformly continuous if for any ε > 0 there exists δ > 0 (depending only on ε) such that d_M(x,y) < δ implies d_N(f(x),f(y)) < ε for all x,y in M.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Definition 8.4.7 — emphasizes δ must work globally, not depend on the point; examples given show contrasts (linear maps are uniformly continuous; x ↦ x^2 on R is not uniformly continuous, but on bounded intervals it is).

rubrics_metrics.name: Heine–Borel for general metric spaces (three equivalent formulations)
rubrics_metrics.description: For a metric space M, the following are equivalent: (i) every sequence has a convergent subsequence (sequential compactness); (ii) M is complete and totally bounded; (iii) every open cover has a finite subcover (quasicompactness).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Theorem 8.5.1 — provides multiple interchangeable criteria for compactness in metric spaces; proofs relate sequential arguments, completeness, total boundedness, and open-cover arguments. See Lemma (Lebesgue number) used in (i),(ii)⇒(iii) direction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lebesgue number lemma for compact metric spaces
rubrics_metrics.description: Let M be a compact metric space and {U_α} an open cover. There exists δ > 0 (a Lebesgue number) such that every δ-neighborhood of any point lies entirely in some U_α.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lemma 8.5.2 — proved by contradiction using sequences and compactness. Consequence: finitely many δ-balls cover M, so finitely many U_α suffice. Important technical tool in many compactness arguments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Counterexample: closed and bounded but not compact (discrete metric)
rubrics_metrics.description: An infinite set S with the discrete metric is closed and bounded but not compact: the sequence s1, s2, ... has no convergent subsequence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example 8.2.5 — demonstrates the necessity of working in R^n for the closed-and-bounded criterion to hold; cautionary example for students to avoid overgeneralizing Heine–Borel.

rubrics_metrics.name: Example of non-compactness via explicit open cover ([0,1) not compact)
rubrics_metrics.description: X = [0,1) is not compact: consider the cover U_m = [0, 1 - 1/(m+1)) for m = 1,2,... ; these cover X but no finite subcollection does.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example 8.3.6 — shows how to craft an open cover with no finite subcover to demonstrate non-compactness; also note sequentially not compact due to the sequence 1 - 1/n failing to converge in [0,1).

rubrics_metrics.name: Module and vector space axioms (requirements for R-module / vector space)
rubrics_metrics.description: An R-module M is an additive abelian group with scalar multiplication satisfying: (i) r1·(r2·m) = (r1 r2)·m; (ii) distributivity across scalars and vectors; (iii) 1_R·m = m; (iv) 0_R·m = 0_M (deducible). If R is a field, M is an R-vector space.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Definition 9.2.5 — provides the precise algebraic conditions a structure must satisfy to be considered a module/vector space; examples include polynomials, R^n, function spaces. Useful as a checklist when verifying a proposed structure is a vector space.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of linear combination, linear independence, spanning, basis
rubrics_metrics.description: A linear combination is r1 v1 + ... + r_n v_n. A set is linearly independent if no nontrivial linear combination equals 0. It is spanning (generating) if every vector is a linear combination of the set. A basis is a set that is both linearly independent and spanning (and coordinates are unique).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Definition 9.4.1 & 9.4.2 — includes the finite-sum proviso for infinite sets; examples and counterexamples given to illustrate failures (non-independence, non-spanning). Basis gives unique coordinate representation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maximality/minimality characterizations of a basis
rubrics_metrics.description: For e1,...,en in V, equivalent statements: (a) they form a basis; (b) they span and no proper subset spans; (c) they are linearly independent and adding any other vector destroys independence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Theorem 9.4.5 — practical checklist: to verify a candidate basis, one may show spanning plus minimality or independence plus maximality. Note caveat: for modules over general rings, some equivalences fail.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dimension theorem for vector spaces (basis cardinality invariance)
rubrics_metrics.description: If V has a finite basis, then every basis has the same number of elements (dimension is well-defined).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Theorem 9.4.7 — proof strategy: compare a spanning set and an independent set and show size inequality; consequences: define dimension, finite-dimensional classification V ≅ k^n.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition and properties of linear maps (homomorphisms)
rubrics_metrics.description: A linear map T : V → W satisfies T(v1+v2) = T(v1)+T(v2) and T(a·v) = a·T(v) for all vectors and scalars. An isomorphism is a bijective linear map.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Definition 9.5.1 and examples 9.5.2 — guidelines: linear maps preserve the vector-space structure; many concrete maps (evaluations, coordinate projections, linear functionals) are given as practice checks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Matrix representation of a linear transform
rubrics_metrics.description: For T : R^n → R^m, the matrix encoding T is obtained by taking the images of the standard basis vectors as the column vectors of an m×n matrix.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Definition 9.6.1 and extended example in R^2 — practical rule: apply the matrix to a coordinate vector to compute T(v); composition corresponds to matrix multiplication; identity map yields identity matrix whose columns are images of basis vectors.
